item.title: DeepMind launches Genie 4 world model enabling unprecedented realism in real-time simulation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: DeepMind has introduced Genie 4, a new generation world model designed to enhance realism in real-time simulations. This advancement represents a significant step forward in the development of AI-driven world simulation technologies. Genie 4 builds on previous models to provide more detailed and accurate representations of complex environments, potentially benefiting applications in gaming, robotics, and virtual reality. The model aims to unlock new possibilities for interactive and dynamic simulations by improving the fidelity and responsiveness of virtual worlds.

item.title: Anthropic reports early progress using Claude AI to accelerate drug development [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Anthropic has shared initial results demonstrating how its Claude AI model can speed up drug development processes. The research highlights the potential of AI to assist in complex biomedical tasks, aiming to reduce time and costs in pharmaceutical research. The company detailed specific applications where Claude helped generate hypotheses and analyze data more efficiently than traditional methods. These early findings suggest AI could become a valuable tool in drug discovery pipelines, though further validation and development are ongoing.

item.title: Survival LLM launches offline AI assistant and emergency library with trusted sources for Mac and Windows [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Survival LLM is a free, open-source AI assistant that runs entirely on a user's computer without internet access, providing emergency information on topics like food safety, first aid, and water purification. It sources answers from a comprehensive library including medical references, government guides, survival manuals, and about 930,000 Wikipedia articles, showing exact source passages for verification. The app adapts to available computer memory by downloading an appropriately sized AI model and requires an initial setup with internet to download the model and library, which can take from 20 minutes to over two hours. It supports adding personal documents for search and maintains privacy by not sending queries online. The software runs on Apple Silicon Macs with macOS 14 or newer and 64-bit Windows 10 or 11, requiring significant disk space for installation.

item.title: Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W and Pi 4 Model A device trees appear in Linux kernel, revealing new board details
item.description: Device tree files for the Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W and Raspberry Pi 4 Model A have been added to the Raspberry Pi Linux kernel source, indicating upcoming new models without official announcements. The Zero 3 W appears to use the Broadcom BCM2711 SoC from the Pi 4, suggesting a significant performance upgrade, while the Pi 4 Model A resembles a stripped-down Pi 4 Model B with fewer ports and no Ethernet. The Zero 3 W device tree hints at features like a single HDMI output, a power button, and possibly eMMC storage, though some details may be placeholders. The Pi 4 Model A lacks Ethernet and analog audio but may support an external antenna, similar to the Compute Module 4. Both boards include SPI flash bootloaders and maintain compatibility with existing GPIO layouts. These findings come from analysis of the device trees and have yet to be confirmed by official Raspberry Pi announcements.

item.title: Researchers formalize the classification of finite simple groups in Lean, uncovering counterexamples in prior proofs and proposing alternative arguments
item.description: A formalization project using the Lean proof assistant has completed the classification of finite simple groups, a major result in group theory. During this process, researchers identified counterexamples to a closure assertion used in an earlier proof approach to the Unbalanced Group Theorem and developed an alternative argument based on Solomon's 1976 theory of maximal 2-components, including a key theorem on the preservation of simple tops. The work is detailed in a 35-page paper titled "The Unbalanced Group Theorem," which explains the obstruction found in the original proof and presents the new approach for the simple-group case. This formalization effort not only verifies the classification but also contributes new insights to the mathematical theory underlying finite simple groups.

item.title: Researchers extend GEPA optimizer to batch candidate proposals for parallel evaluation, achieving up to fourfold speedups and improved test scores on LiveBench-Math and HoVer tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have enhanced the open-source GEPA optimizer by enabling it to propose and evaluate multiple candidates in parallel during each optimization step, rather than sequentially. This approach reduces wall-clock time significantly-most batched runs completed in half the time or less, with the fastest finishing in about a quarter to a third of the original time-and improves held-out test performance on two benchmark tasks, LiveBench-Math and HoVer. The team developed a runtime model explaining the speedups under a limited worker pool and found that batched optimization uses metric-call and budget resources more efficiently. Their work also outlines the dimensions along which reflective optimization can scale in parallel, providing a framework for allocating fixed optimization budgets across these axes.

item.title: Prospector trains a compact model to traverse scientific knowledge graphs for reasoning, outperforming off-the-shelf models and transferring across domains [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Prospector is a compact model trained to perform step-by-step traversal of domain-specific knowledge graphs to support scientific reasoning, addressing limitations of large language models that lack proprietary or specialized data. It progressively builds context by calling a small set of tools and produces evidence chains that can be verified against the graph, achieving performance close to top models on a semiconductor manufacturing knowledge graph and surpassing models that rely on closed-book or preselected graph portions. Although trained only on semiconductor data, Prospector successfully transfers its traversal policy to knowledge graphs from bio-inspired materials, PFAS, and materials properties fields. It runs efficiently on a single GPU, reducing costs and keeping proprietary data on local hardware. The model's latent state guides its traversal decisions and can be modulated to alter behavior, suggesting a practical approach for combining large language models with knowledge graphs to enable scientific and engineering reasoning over private data.

item.title: MedJev evaluates zero-shot System One decision model for medical tasks, achieving near GPT-4 accuracy on benchmarks and strong patient-level mortality prediction with local recalibration [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: MedJev is an open System One decision model designed for fast, efficient clinical support by answering structured medical questions without text generation. It was tested across ten medical benchmarks including MedQA, USMLE, and NEJM, achieving accuracies close to GPT-4 and outperforming some supervised models on patient mortality prediction using MIMIC IV datasets. The model runs locally on a laptop and maintains well-calibrated confidence estimates for knowledge tasks but shows miscalibration on patient-level predictions, which the authors address with a lightweight recalibration method using limited labeled data. This work establishes open System One models as promising zero-shot baselines for medical AI, balancing competitive performance with low computational cost, and the authors have released their code and evaluation tools to support further research.

item.title: Researchers present Fin-SD, a hindsight self-distillation method for multi-step financial reasoning that improves accuracy without external teachers by using student-generated critiques [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Fin-SD, a localized hindsight self-distillation technique designed to enhance multi-step financial reasoning in models constrained by data residency. Fin-SD has the student model identify its first incorrect reasoning step, generate a critique, and then distill a hint-conditioned frozen copy of itself to improve accuracy without relying on external teachers. Applied to GPT-OSS-20B on a financial reasoning benchmark, Fin-SD achieves a 3.03 percentage point accuracy gain over the base model and matches traditional self-distillation methods while generating 9.5% fewer tokens. The study finds that the location of supervision matters more than the hint content, and that stronger models do not necessarily provide better hints. Fin-SD maintains performance on general reasoning and compliance audits without regression.

item.title: Researchers show base pre-trained models can detect hidden intentions in outputs that prompted classifiers miss using persona-header likelihood evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose the Persona Selection Model (PSM) and introduce persona-header likelihood evaluation (PHLE) to decode subliminal signals embedded in model outputs, such as number sequences reflecting covert prompts like "You love owls" versus "You love eagles." PHLE distinguishes these signals even when prompted classifiers, including the generating model, perform near chance. The method also detects hidden harmful intents in filtered model responses and shows signal persistence across different model families, suggesting practical applications for auditing hidden model objectives.

item.title: RoboAuto introduces a multi-level physical understanding framework for autonomous robot program search, achieving up to 89.1% success on LIBERO-PRO tasks and outperforming prior methods on long-horizon manipulation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: RoboAuto is a new framework for autonomous robot program search that integrates physical understanding at the object, scene, and interaction levels. It uses a hierarchical knowledge base combining executable skills with object-centric knowledge, scene grounding to connect knowledge to the environment, and multi-stage planning with self-designed experiments to test physical effects and resolve uncertainties. This approach enables superior performance on five benchmark families, including an 89.1% success rate on short-horizon LIBERO-PRO tasks and more than double the success rate of ASPIRE on long-horizon LIBERO-PRO Long and LIBERO-Plus tasks. RoboAuto also outperforms ASPIRE and π₀.₅ on challenging real-robot tasks requiring precise manipulation. The knowledge base transfers across simulators and robot embodiments, and program search performance improves with knowledge base size.

item.title: Researchers propose Balanced State Subspaces and HARP for Mamba-2 state compression, halving state dimension with minimal perplexity increase on WikiText-2 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce a post-training transform called Balanced State Subspaces for Mamba-2, a model that compresses context into a fixed-size recurrent state dominating decoding memory and bandwidth. They find that existing compression methods miss key directions in the state space and propose targeting the write-read subspace instead. To address varying useful ranks across layers, they also introduce HARP, which allocates ranks per layer based on the Hankel spectrum and protects retrieval-sensitive layers, improving perplexity and retrieval performance compared to uniform budgets. The proposed method applies balanced truncation using full controllability and observability Gramians and leverages Mamba-2's scalar-identity transition for exact rotation. Calibration requires only a single forward pass, making it significantly faster and more memory-efficient than previous protocols like GHOST. Experiments show that with HARP, the state dimension can be halved with an average perplexity increase of 0.3 points (1.8%) on WikiText-2 across model sizes from 130 million to 2.7 billion parameters, outperforming GHOST's 1.6 point (9.3%) increase, with the performance gap widening at 25% retention.

item.title: Researchers train small GPT-2 models on child speech transcripts and synthetic dialogues to study language learning from limited, naturalistic data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers trained small GPT-2 language models on transcripts of child speech from dense home recordings and synthetic child-directed dialogues, varying the amount, source, and diversity of training data to investigate language learning from small datasets. Models trained on one child's language environment predicted that environment better than others, with specialization largely lexical and distributional, and training on multiple children's data improved prediction of pooled language but not grammatical benchmarks. The study found that naturalistic and synthetic inputs produce different grammatical and lexical-semantic patterns, highlighting that small-data language learning depends on both the quantity and the match of input environments to the prediction task.

item.title: Select-TTT introduces query-conditioned selective fast weight updates for in-place test-time training, improving long-context question answering on multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Select-TTT is a new method that enhances in-place test-time training (TTT) for language models by selectively scaling fast weight updates based on the relevance of context chunks to the user query. Unlike previous uniform update approaches, Select-TTT uses a relevance signal derived from the model's frozen output head without additional parameters or supervision. This approach consistently improves performance on long-context question answering tasks across different benchmarks and model backbones. The method maintains efficient chunk-wise, context-parallel computation and shows promise for applications involving multiple user queries over evolving contexts.

item.title: Researchers introduce V-LUMEN, a visual lookup memory system that discretizes visual features to expand capacity in vision-language models without increasing compute [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: V-LUMEN is a new approach that applies embedding-level scaling to vision-language models by discretizing continuous visual features using a frozen codebook and spatially aware hashing. It integrates retrieved embeddings into model backbones through a gated residual pathway, improving performance on reasoning-intensive benchmarks and enabling zero-shot transfer to unseen image datasets. The method maintains accuracy while shifting capacity from adapters to external visual memory, which grows storage requirements rather than per-token computation, and the code has been made publicly available.

item.title: Researchers propose EvidenceConnect framework to improve multimodal perception by training vision-language models on synthesized data linking visual evidence within images [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce EvidenceConnect, a data synthesis framework that generates questions requiring comparison and aggregation of visual evidence from zoomed regions within single images to enhance multimodal perception. They train vision-language models using this data with reinforcement learning, resulting in Zooming without Zooming v2 (ZwZ2), which improves fine-grained spatial perception and multimodal reasoning tasks without being tailored to specific benchmarks. The approach demonstrates that strengthening the capability to connect visual evidence leads to more generalizable multimodal intelligence.

item.title: Researchers find single-pair model biases limit Direct Preference Optimization performance compared to multi-model data, highlighting generator diversity as key [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers investigated the delta-learning hypothesis in Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), which suggests supervision can come from a single pair of models by preferring the larger model's response. They found that fixed model pairs introduce systematic biases that predict preference labels independent of response quality, causing DPO trained on single-pair data to underperform compared to multi-model preference data despite higher-quality responses from larger models. The study combined theoretical and empirical analysis across model families and scales, tracing performance gaps to training dynamics consistent with reward hacking on these biases. Increasing the number of generators, even without an external judge, partially mitigated these effects, underscoring the importance of generator diversity in constructing preference data for DPO.

item.title: Researchers introduce EnergyCal to reduce loss spikes in Muon-family optimizers for sparse MoE training, achieving over 95% spike reduction on a 4B-parameter model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present EnergyCal, a lightweight method that attenuates routed-expert updates based on normalized squared Frobenius norms to stabilize sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language-model training with Muon-family optimizers. Evaluated on a 4-billion-parameter MoE model, EnergyCal reduced mean thresholded loss-spike burden by 99.51% and improved final perplexity by 4.06% compared to a lower-learning-rate MuonH baseline, with modest throughput cost. The method does not alter the spectral transform or add persistent optimizer state. Results also show over 95% spike reduction with plain Muon optimizer at matched learning rates, supporting stabilization both with and without Hyperball in the tested setting.

item.title: Researchers propose EvalAlloc framework to optimize evaluation budget allocation in LLM-driven agent scaffold evolution, achieving higher performance with half the evaluations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers investigate how to allocate evaluation budgets in large language model (LLM)-driven agent scaffold evolution, which improves agent workflows through iterative candidate generation and evaluation but incurs high execution costs when evaluating every candidate fully. They find that sparse feedback can sustain productive evolution, while targeted evaluation enhances final selection, and propose EvalAlloc, a framework combining sparse search-time feedback with targeted final confirmation to optimize evaluation efficiency. EvalAlloc uses a short fully evaluated warm-up to establish a shared informative core and calibrate a response model, then applies paired successive halving after search to reuse observations and execute only missing evaluations. Tested across four benchmarks and two evolution frameworks, EvalAlloc achieves higher mean performance than full evaluation in most settings while using approximately half as many evaluation cells, indicating a more efficient approach to managing evaluation costs in LLM-driven agent development.

item.title: Researchers develop SimpleLoRIF to trace safety degradation in fine-tuned LLMs by identifying training examples aligned with unsafe behavior, enabling safer dataset filtering [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed SimpleLoRIF, a scalable gradient embedding method that identifies fine-tuning examples in large language models (LLMs) whose gradients align with unsafe behavior, addressing the challenge of safety degradation from seemingly benign training data. By simplifying a low-rank attribution method and limiting backpropagation to the final transformer blocks, SimpleLoRIF can process datasets with up to a million examples, making gradient attribution practical for full post-training datasets. The team validated SimpleLoRIF on emergent misalignment scenarios, showing it can link insecure-code training data to harmful behaviors after fine-tuning with high accuracy. Using this method, they created SafeTulu, a filtered version of Tulu 3 that removes the 20% of examples most aligned with unsafe responses, reducing attack success rates by up to 22% across multiple models while maintaining or improving capabilities. The researchers also identified under-studied sources of safety issues, such as tool-execution failures and narrative arithmetic, and released SafeTulu along with a Hugging Face Space for customizable dataset filtering and fine-tuning.

item.title: Validating FKG.in: Soundness Assessment in LLM-Augmented Indian Food Knowledge [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.29249v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The online culinary ecosystem is increasingly populated by recipe content generated, modified, or summarized by LLMs. Although often convincing, such outputs may contain hallucinated ingredients, misrepresented quantities, or culturally implausible combinations, limiting their suitability for downstream applications and knowledge graph construction. In this paper, we present a semi-automated soundness assessment workflow for validating structured recipe data extracted from informal culinary sources and augmented by LLMs. Developed as part of FKG(.in), a knowledge graph of Indian food, the pipeline identifies and addresses common failure modes, including structural inconsistencies, semantic and logical incoherence, and deviations from the source text, through a multi-stage process combining formal grammars, vocabulary-based checks, statistical heuristics, Set Transformer-based coherence modeling, and retrieval-based verification. Although evaluated on Indian recipes, the proposed methods are applicable to broader multilingual and multicultural culinary domains. We provide a practical, auditable, and application-agnostic approach to improving the reliability of machine-readable food knowledge infrastructures in the era of LLM-generated content.

item.title: Fairness Definitions in Language Models Explained [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2407.18454v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language Models (LMs) have demonstrated exceptional performance across various Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. Despite these advancements, LMs can inherit and amplify societal biases related to sensitive attributes such as gender and race, limiting their adoption in real-world applications. Therefore, fairness has been extensively explored in LMs, leading to the proposal of various fairness notions. However, the lack of clear agreement on which fairness definition to apply in specific contexts and the complexity of understanding the distinctions between these definitions can create confusion and impede further progress. To this end, this paper proposes a systematic survey that clarifies the definitions of fairness as they apply to LMs. Specifically, we begin with a brief introduction to LMs and fairness in LMs, followed by a comprehensive, up-to-date overview of existing fairness notions in LMs and the introduction of a novel taxonomy that categorizes these concepts based on their transformer architecture: encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder LMs. We further illustrate each definition through experiments, showcasing their practical implications and outcomes. Finally, we discuss current research challenges and open questions, aiming to foster innovative ideas and advance the field. The repository is publicly available online at https://github.com/vanbanTruong/Fairness-in-Large-Language-Models/tree/main/definitions.

item.title: An Embarrassingly Simple Data Selection Strategy for Million-Scale Multi-Modal Instruction-Tuning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2503.13383v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent research demonstrates that pretrained large language models (LLMs) require minimal but carefully curated data for instruction-tuning. Building on LLMs, multi-modal models further contend with far larger data volumes, heterogeneous sources, and cross-modal alignment, amplifying both the necessity and the complexity of data selection. However, existing methods rely on deeply extracted embeddings, gradients or narrow quality scores that are time-consuming to compute and limited in expressiveness, frequently failing to surpass a simple random-sampling baseline. To overcome these limitations, we step back from complex embedding spaces and target the fundamental objective of instruction tuning: how and what knowledge should be elicited from the pretrained model and exposed to users. We leverage interaction \underline{S}tyles as a proxy for structural diversity, and decompose data quality into capability-specific \underline{S}cores, yielding an explicit yet \underline{R}ich (SSR) profile for each sample. We further cast the selection as submodular coverage maximization over the capability--style grid, providing an approximation guarantee. SSR consistently delivers superior performance across two distinct architecture stacks, LLaVA-1.5 (Vicuna + CLIP) and LLaVA-OneVision (Qwen2 + SigLIP), two large-scale data pools, six data budget settings, and 14 multi-modal benchmarks. To our knowledge, SSR is the first data selection method validated at million-scale, achieving 99.1% of full-data performance using only 30% of a 2.6M pool. Furthermore, the SSR profile models and selected subsets transfer training-free across data pools and model architectures with capability extensibility.

item.title: SELF: A Robust Singular Value and Eigenvalue Approach for LLM Fingerprinting [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2512.03620v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Safeguarding the Intellectual Property (IP) of Large Language Models (LLMs) against model theft represents a critical challenge in contemporary AI research. Although fingerprinting is essential for establishing forensic evidence for model derivation, existing methods are susceptible to false claim attacks, weight manipulations, or high false positive rates, undermining their utility. To overcome these limitations, we propose SELF, \rev{a novel intrinsic weight-based fingerprinting scheme tailored for robust IP forensics via adversarial model lineage verification}. SELF eliminates dependency on input and inherently resists false claims, achieving robust \rev{provenance detection} through unique, scalable and transformation-invariant fingerprint extraction via singular value and eigenvalue decomposition of LLM attention weights. Experimental results demonstrate that SELF maintains high IP infringement detection accuracy while significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in reducing false positives and showing strong robustness against various downstream modifications, including quantization, pruning, and fine-tuning attacks. Our code is available at https://github.com/HanxiuZhang/SELF_v4.

item.title: Counting Clues: A Lightweight Probabilistic Baseline Can Match an LLM [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2512.12868v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel on multiple-choice clinical diagnosis benchmarks, yet it is unclear how much of this performance reflects underlying probabilistic reasoning. We study this through questions from MedQA that ask for the most likely diagnosis. We introduce Frequency-Based Probabilistic Ranker (FBPR), a lightweight method that scores options with a smoothed Naive Bayes over concept-diagnosis co-occurrence statistics from a large corpus. When co-occurrence statistics are sourced from Dolma, the pretraining corpus for OLMo, and RedPajama, an open reproduction of the LLaMA pretraining-data recipe, FBPR achieves comparable performance to the corresponding LLMs. Furthermore, direct LLM inference and FBPR exhibit complementary strengths, correctly answering largely different subsets of questions with overlap barely above chance. Combining them with a simple hybrid method yields a notable gain over either method alone. These findings show that explicit probabilistic baselines can account for a substantial portion of the benchmark performance on diagnosis questions, while serving as historically grounded reference points and complementary signals for hybridization.

item.title: The Geometry of Learning: Read-Write Asymmetry Across Training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2605.16600v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pretraining and alignment update the same transformer weights, and we ask in which directions each stage changes them. The residual stream gives every matrix a shared coordinate system, in which a weight change can be compared with the principal subspace of the activations the matrix reads and with the prediction subspace of the unembedding. In this frame, alignment updates to the query and key matrices are enriched in the principal input subspace, while its updates to the output matrices are close to random relative to the prediction subspace, and the same signature appears in late pretraining and under every objective we apply to one checkpoint, so it is a property of the training stage rather than of the objective. The gradient of a linear map is a sum of outer products $\delta_t a_t^\top$, and the residual stream enters this product through the activation $a_t$ for matrices that read from it and through the upstream gradient $\delta_t$ for matrices that write into it. Read gradients therefore inherit the spectrum of the activations, which is the same under every objective, while write gradients inherit the geometry of the upstream gradients, which point into the prediction subspace only early in pretraining, when the output matrices acquire their prediction geometry. The raw read gradient follows the activation spectrum, the optimiser attenuates the concentration it inherits, and cancellation between tokens sets the scale of the update but not its direction. A write direction derived from the unembedding still changes predictions after alignment, and adaptation restricted to any single group of matrices remains effective, so the signature describes where training places its updates, not which matrices can carry them.

item.title: Does The Way You Plan Matter? An Empirical Study of Planning Representations for LLM Web Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2605.29927v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Despite recent advances, LLM-based web agents still struggle with limited exploration, omission of critical steps, and sensitivity to task constraints. Prior work suggests that many of these failures stem from weaknesses in planning, yet the impact of alternative natural language plan representations remains unexplored. To address this, we introduce PlanAhead, a static planner-executor framework that evaluates the impact of plan representation on agent performance. We first automatically categorize WebArena tasks into 3 difficulty levels, enabling consistent difficulty grading without human annotation. Then we systematically evaluate 4 different plan representations on the tasks categorized as hard: sequential subgoals, narrative, pseudocode, and checklist; across different families of multimodal LLM-powered agents(OpenAI, Alibaba, and Google). To account for stochastic variability, we introduce a novel decomposition of agent Success Rate (SR) into 2 interpretable evaluation metrics: Achievement Rate (AR) and Solved-Task Consistency (STC). Our results show that both, the plan formulation and the underlying LLM generating the plan, significantly influence web-agent robustness and task success.

item.title: TextCloak: Safeguarding Data from Unauthorized LLM Fine-Tuning via RL-Driven Unlearnable Examples [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.28862v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The development of Large Language Models (LLMs) has led to significant advances across a wide range of language tasks, while simultaneously raising growing concerns about unauthorized online data exploitation and privacy leakage. Unlearnable examples (UEs) emerge as a promising defense by injecting crafted perturbations into data such that models trained on them exhibit degraded utility. However, existing methods for text protection are primarily designed for classification tasks and discriminative language models, which limits their broad applicability (e.g., instruction following or reasoning) in LLMs. In this work, we propose **TextCloak**, an RL-driven data synthesis framework that safeguards textual data against unauthorized LLM fine-tuning. TextCloak employs a *UE generative policy* that transforms clean text into unlearnable examples while preserving semantic fidelity and linguistic naturalness. To optimize the policy, we introduce **GRPO-UE**, which simulates the attacker's LLM fine-tuning and rewards downstream degradation via group-relative policy optimization. This overall formulates a bi-level optimization loop, allowing the generator to discover effective protective patterns. Comprehensive experiments on six publicly available datasets and nine state-of-the-art LLMs demonstrate that TextCloak consistently impairs unauthorized LLM fine-tuning while maintaining text utility for legitimate use. Further analyses confirm its transferability and robustness across model architectures, training configurations, and adaptive attacks, highlighting its broad applicability as a practical defense for online content.

item.title: The Score Is Not the Structure: Brain Alignment and Cross-Lingual Transfer [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.03827v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Similarity scores are often offered as evidence that a model shares structure with the brain or across languages. We ask what such a score reads when that structure is removed, or when the instrument measuring it does not work, in two settings. Across seventeen languages, a grammaticality probe transfers worse between more distant languages (r = -0.66). But the probe's own accuracy falls along the same axis and is at chance in four languages, four of the five most distant. Dropping them halves the explained variance, and because it also narrows the range of distances, the design cannot say how much of the gradient is the instrument. Counting the 272 language pairs as independent gives p = 0.0006 for a steering effect that is null when the seventeen languages are the unit (p = 0.155). In brain alignment, a training objective raises a language model's similarity to fMRI responses from 0.10 to 0.34 (reliability ceiling 0.54), yet targets with the brain correspondence destroyed still reach 0.31. A shuffled target scores about k/n against the real one, for rank k and n sentences, a baseline that can be computed before any model is trained. Both interventions work, yet we detect no distance-graded steering effect and no syntactic benefit from alignment. Before reading a correspondence score, measure how much of it survives without the correspondence.

item.title: Agaram 2.5B: The First Tamil-First Language Model Trained from Scratch with Tool Calling. A Playbook for Under-Represented Languages [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.18420v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present Agaram 2.5B, a Tamil-first language model trained from scratch that converses in Tamil script, romanized Tanglish and English, and calls tools. Our first model, Agaram 1.5B, guided the new base, tokenizer and fine-tuning recipe: we pretrained a new 2.53B-parameter base on 50 billion tokens, 58% of them Tamil, with a tokenizer that needs 1.55 tokens per Tamil word where Qwen2.5's needs 9.44. A four-day public preview of our first 2.5B chat model showed where it fell short with real users, and we rebuilt supervised fine-tuning around what we saw, on 222,662 records. The released model scores above Sarvam-1 in all six translation directions we measured (FLORES chrF 56.9 into Tamil and 55.4 into English), chooses the expected tool on all 25 prompts of a tool set that was used during checkpoint selection and whose schemas appear in training, with exact arguments on 16, and was preferred over the preview model by an LLM judge on 100 sealed human-written prompts (net preference +30 points, 95% interval +14.5 to +45.0). On FLORES it also scores above Google's Gemma 4 E4B-it and our fine-tuned variant of it in both directions, with 2.53B parameters against E4B's 4.5B effective parameters. Factual knowledge and reliable refusal of harmful requests remain open problems, which we set out as future work. The base and chat weights and GGUF files are released under Apache-2.0, and this report gives a full account of the data, training and evaluation as a playbook for building language models for under-represented languages.

item.title: Quantitative Generalization Bounds for Multi-Layer Transformers: A Few Long Strings can Beat Many Short Ones [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.35715v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Transformer-based language models exhibit an astonishing capacity to generalize to longer and more difficult problem instances than those seen in training. However, theoretical understanding of this phenomenon still lags behind. Unlike most machine learning models, the generalisation abilities of transformers inherently require considering two axes. On one hand, one must examine in-distribution statistical generalisation, which concerns the ability of a model to broaden a function from training samples to novel samples of the same distribution. On the other hand, given the sequential nature of language data, one must also consider length generalisation, which reflects whether a model trained on inputs of a given length can extrapolate to longer ones. These two notions have mostly been studied separately, leaving open how they interact. In this work, we give a joint treatment of both axes for fixed-precision transformers. We give generalisation guarantees in terms of the parameter sizes of the involved models, as well as the quantization space and the alphabet size that supply the sequences. Finally, we illustrate how the requirements in the sample count and training length trade off. In particular, we find that increasing training length can be exponentially more efficient than increasing the sample size. Experiments support predictions of the theory.

item.title: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
Don't Pick a Winner: Knowledge Conflicts Need a Prior, Not a Rule [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36169v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A retrieval-augmented language model answers from two sources, the retrieved context and its own knowledge, and the two disagree whenever the context is incomplete or wrong. Existing methods settle the disagreement with a rule fixed at design time: follow the context, amplify it in proportion to how far it moves the model, or trust the model's memory. Each rule is confidently wrong in some deployment. In a decision-theoretic model of two sources, the score of any fixed rule is linear in the share of reliable contexts while the best attainable score is convex, so every fixed rule is beaten wherever it is not exactly optimal; and a symmetric divergence between the two sources, the signal adaptive decoding uses, carries no information about which one is right. Resolving a conflict therefore needs two inputs that no existing method keeps: evidence about each source separately, and a prior on how often the context is right. We test these claims on GRACE, a benchmark that intervenes on the knowledge-graph context of a fixed question, so that what the model knows, what the context says and what is true are measured separately. There, every baseline from four families is strong on right contexts or on wrong ones, never on both. We then build the two inputs: the model states its knowledge as notes, a small policy voices each note with a calibrated confidence, a reader answers in two voices, and a selector commits or abstains under a prior $\pi$ applied as an exact prior shift. With $\pi$ set to the true share of right contexts, the system is above the best baseline at every mixture of GRACE contexts, by up to 26 points. Its overall score is 45.3 and 35.0 (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, Llama-3.1-8B), against 29.4 and 27.5 for the best baseline. On preregistered ClashEval it beats same-backbone CK-PLUG and TCR by 12 and 26 points. Where the model lacks the knowledge, the gains vanish, as the theory predicts.

item.title: A Heart Means Recursion: Exploring Visual Meaning and Communication in VLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36449v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Do vision-language models (VLMs) share our ability to communicate visually? We share preliminary findings, starting from a surprising observation: simple visual symbols like a red heart can strongly influence model behavior on seemingly unrelated tasks, such as steering models towards recursive solutions on simple coding problems. Notably, this steering effect is largely implicit, as models' direct interpretations and thinking traces about visual symbols diverge substantially from their observed behavior. In visual communication between models, this leads to a generation--interpretation gap: while models tend to send shape primitives that they (and humans) find intuitive, these visual cues often fail to steer other models. In further communication games involving abstract concepts and stories, models can creatively use visuals to transmit meaning to one another, although some communications remain non-intuitive to humans. These findings reveal that VLMs might be capable of rich, creative, and visually-grounded communication, but their interpretation and production of visual meaning diverges from human conventions in surprising ways. Together this work highlights both the promise and challenges of visual communication between humans and VLMs.

item.title: AC-JEPA: Anchored Cross-Modal Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture for Visual-to-Symbolic Translation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36493v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cross-modal translation requires models to capture shared semantics across modalities while preserving the fine-grained structure required by the target modality. Yet in real-world scientific domains, paired data are often imperfect, while obtaining clean pairs at scale is costly. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) directly optimizes cross-modal translation through categorical token-level supervision, but this objective is sensitive to errors in the target sequences. JEPA offers a complementary representation-space objective, but most existing formulations focus on prediction within a modality rather than translation across modalities. We introduce Anchored Cross-Modal JEPA (AC-JEPA), an SFT-compatible plug-in that predicts masked intermediate states in both cross-modal directions using paired data. The joint-embedding objective targets cross-modal structure predictable from context, while the causal SFT path retains direct token-level supervision for the target sequence. During self-training, AC-JEPA learns from continuous latent targets derived from imperfect pseudo-labeled pairs, offering intrinsic tolerance to local data errors without promoting pseudo-tokens to hard categorical supervision. Using optical chemical structure recognition as a testbed, AC-JEPA trained on clean pairs achieves 76.07% accuracy on the Simple set of the WildMol benchmark, compared with 67.40% for SFT alone. Using the same pseudo-labeled data for both approaches, AC-JEPA-based self-training further raises accuracy to 80.23%, whereas accuracy under direct SFT drops from 67.40% to 63.47%. These results support SFT-anchored joint-embedding prediction as an effective strategy for cross-modal translation under both curated and imperfect supervision.

item.title: MedConstBench: Benchmarking How Constitutions Steer LLMs in Medical Ethics [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models advance rapidly, they are increasingly used to answer medical questions, and many such models are now deployed locally. Once a model is deployed, its behavior is governed mainly by the ethical policy written into its constitution. However, most existing work focuses on factual correctness rather than the trade-off between competing ethical values. Even benchmarks that do evaluate ethics treat it as a fixed property of the model rather than as a variable, so how a constitution reshapes medical-ethics behavior remains largely unexplored. We introduce MedConstBench, a medical-ethics benchmark that treats the deployment constitution as a controlled variable, is organized around Beauchamp's four principles, and is scored by human-calibrated multi-model peer review. It includes MedDilemma, our own dataset of clinical dilemmas, and supports a systematic analysis of how constitutions steer LLMs. Evaluating ten open-source LLMs under four constitutions, we find that the effect of a constitution is dimension-selective and model-dependent, and that no constitution is universally optimal. Motivated by these findings, we propose a do-no-harm adaptive selector that chooses a constitution per model, matching the per-model oracle while guaranteeing a worst-case floor and generalizing to unseen models at low cost.

item.title: God Does Not Play Dice: Enforcing Batch Invariance in Agentic Kernel Generation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving systems dynamically batch user requests for GPU execution, so the same request may be processed alongside different requests across runs. If the GPU kernels lack batch invariance (BI), this changing batch context can alter the numerical output for an unchanged input, undermining reproducibility. Existing kernel generation agents focus on correctness and efficiency but \emph{overlook BI}. We find 19 confirmed BI violations among 83 batch-applicable released artifacts. To address this limitation, we propose \tool, which combines contract-guided static dependency analysis with dynamic validation of bitwise consistency across batch contexts. \tool is designed as a plug-in component for general kernel agents, allowing their original optimization capabilities to be reused while adding BI enforcement. We integrate it as successive acceptance gates in the optimization loop, rejecting structurally risky or dynamically non-invariant candidates before performance benchmarking and returning feedback to the agent. Experiments across three agent frameworks under baseline and BI-aware generation on real world LLM serving tasks show that \tool improves the BI pass rate from 67.6\% to 91.9\% while retaining 91.8\% of the baseline geometric mean speedup. These results demonstrate that \tool can be incorporated into kernel optimization by agents as an additional reliability objective alongside correctness and speed.

item.title: GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36877v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mobile GUI agents are typically fine-tuned 7B-scale vision-language models (VLMs) that generate each action as text. However, these VLMs decode every action token by token, and even agents that score candidate actions keep a large language model or VLM in the loop, making them slow and memory-hungry. To address these issues, we propose GUI-JEPA, to our knowledge the first decoder-free GUI agent policy built on a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), which selects actions in the latent space of a JEPA encoder pretrained on unlabelled GUI screenshots. Its action- and region-conditioned latent predictor turns the screen latent into one latent per candidate action, letting lightweight heads score all candidates against the instruction in a single batched pass, without decoding a token. We further show that the scorer relies on this latent pathway and that the predictor is trained for the decision itself: a randomly initialised predictor does just as well as one pretrained on screen dynamics. On AndroidControl, GUI-JEPA is 2.8-4.0x faster on the same GPU than a Qwen2.5-VL-7B agent we fine-tune with the same inputs, while reaching 86-92% of its in-distribution accuracy with 6% of its parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/bcwang-sjtu/GUI-JEPA

item.title: RubricAtlas: Mining Type-Level Rubrics from Expert Reports to Evaluate Deep Research Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36878v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep research agents conduct multi-step Web searches and synthesise retrieved information into analytical reports. Evaluating these outputs requires checking which analyses they deliver, beyond the presence of relevant facts. Query-specific binary rubrics make individual requirements explicit, but task-level checklists may leave the overall analytical structure underexamined. We introduce RubricAtlas, which derives type-level analytical requirements from expert reports on different objects within the same research type and organises detailed checks around recurring analytical questions. The requirements give related tasks a shared standard for what to analyse, without prescribing their answers. Our framework links binary checkpoints to report passages and evaluates completeness separately from argument validity. Built from 3,079 Chinese financial research reports, RubricAtlas covers 99 research types. Reference-report selection experiments show that individual reports cover only about half of their type's analytical questions, and that selecting requirements from different reports changes evaluation scores and agent rankings. Across ten agents, two judge pipelines achieve checkpoint agreement of $\kappa$ = 0.71 and agent-ranking agreement of Kendall $\tau$ = 0.87. Controlled deletions reduce scores on the affected analyses, while padding produces no detectable increase. These findings support type-level rubrics for comparing the analytical completeness of Web deep research outputs, with individual decisions traceable to report evidence.

item.title: AutoVend: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Autonomous Vending Operations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are extending agent-mediated commerce on the Web from shopping for consumers to operating businesses for sellers. In online-to-offline (O2O) commerce, decisions are issued through Web-based platforms but realized through costly physical execution. Evaluating such agents requires going beyond individual transactions to ask whether decisions made online turn into sustained economic returns. We introduce AutoVend, a benchmark in which one LLM agent manages 20 vending machines across five site types through a Web-based operating interface for 180 simulated days. Its data-grounded simulator combines a shared warehouse, procurement lead times, paid replenishment, inventory expiration, and recurring operating costs. We evaluate five LLM agents against a rule-based inventory-control baseline and diagnose their site coordination, execution, and performance over time. Four of five evaluated LLM agents fall short of this baseline, and returns per dollar of inference cost rank models differently from returns alone. Operational analyses show that gains in individual metrics do not consistently yield stronger economic growth, as inventory and execution costs erode these gains. Trajectory analysis further reveals difficulties in grounding feasible actions, managing inventory commitments, and converting feedback into effective policy revisions.

item.title: SpectRAG: Weighted Chunk Graphs for Token-Budgeted Context Selection in Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36991v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems ground large language models (LLMs) by retrieving external evidence and conditioning generation on the retrieved context. Although dense retrieval is effective for local semantic matching, independently ranked retrieval can return redundant passages, miss cross-chunk dependencies, and provide incomplete evidence for multi-hop reasoning. We propose SpectRAG, a spectral graph-augmented retrieval framework that combines hybrid candidate seeding, weighted chunk graph construction, graph-based expansion, spectral relevance propagation, and token-budgeted context selection. Document chunks are represented by dense semantic embeddings and graph-spectral coordinates derived from a weighted chunk graph whose edges encode semantic similarity, document adjacency, section hierarchy, shared entities, citation links, and similarity between LLM-generated utility questions. At query time, SpectRAG builds a high-recall seed set using exact inner-product search and hybrid relevance signals, expands it over the chunk graph, re-scores candidates using graph proximity and spectral information, and assembles the final context under a fixed token budget. The goal is not merely to retrieve individually similar chunks, but to construct a context that is relevant, diverse, structurally connected, and sufficient for grounded reasoning. Experiments on MultiHopRAG, UltraDomain, and long-document question-answering settings show that SpectRAG improves broad evidence recovery and achieves competitive generation quality against dense, hybrid, HyDE, LightRAG, and NaiveRAG baselines. The results further indicate that graph-spectral structure is particularly useful for inference-oriented and cross-document retrieval, while highlighting trade-offs in early precision, computational cost, and domain-dependent performance.

item.title: Guided-RLVR: Guided Exploration in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.37041v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has shown strong empirical gains in improving the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs) on tasks such as mathematics and programming. However, recent studies have shown that RLVR rollouts often collapse onto a narrow set of reasoning trajectories, limiting the explored reasoning space. Motivated by findings that thinking tokens at critical steps serve as critical structural elements in LLM reasoning pathways, we propose Guided-RLVR, a novel approach that augments RLVR with a lightweight controller. The controller strategically injects semantically meaningful steering tokens into the sampling distribution, encouraging the model to approach problems from multiple reasoning perspectives and thereby expanding the exploration space. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks show that Guided-RLVR consistently outperforms existing RLVR methods while producing more diverse reasoning trajectories.

item.title: Agent-Conditioned Routing: Diverse Reasoning Paths Within One Frozen Model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.37375v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generating several solutions can expose alternative methods, but additional trajectories often paraphrase one dominant approach. We investigate whether the conditional capacity of a frozen sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) model can provide such diversity from one problem prompt, without user-assigned roles, prescribed methods, fine-tuning, or model copies. Agent-Conditioned Routing (ACR) assigns $m$ parallel trajectories persistent, untrained shared/private expert-eligibility masks while preserving the learned, input-dependent token router. On a screened 126-question multi-mode mathematics and physics benchmark, with model judges reading the reported derivations in full, we count the number of problems yielding at least two distinct primary methods among soft-correct solutions in four trajectories. ACR reaches approximately twice as many such problems as the strongest temperature setting under GLM 5.3 (37.3 versus 18.7), and 1.67 times as many under GPT-5.6 Sol (45.00 versus 27.00), at matched output budgets. A blinded four-expert audit on a stratified sample of 30 problems also finds more multi-method solutions with ACR on both backbones, with lower correctness. Matched-eligibility ablations show modest multi-method count advantages for ACR, while token-resampled masks attain higher correctness. An informed sequential prompt elicits more diversity still, using previous solutions and explicit requests for alternative methods. ACR adds about 160 KiB of mask state. In a three-problem microbenchmark capped at 1,024 tokens, its latency and peak VRAM usage remain within 3% of batched temperature sampling.

item.title: Rare, Relevant, and Still Wrong: How Memory Fails LLM Group Decisions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.37624v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When an LLM group's discussion is compressed into a short memory for a final decision maker, what should the memory keep? Two natural heuristics keep the rarest claims or the claims relevant to the decision criteria. On hidden-profile tasks both look attractive, because how widely a fact is held is confounded with whether it helps. We introduce CrossProfile, a diagnostic benchmark of 60 templates with automatically verified answer keys, in which the ownership of supporting, decoy, and irrelevant facts is crossed while their text is held fixed (480 tasks). Across Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and two DeepSeek models, both heuristics fail in predictable places. Selecting by relevance readmits decoys, because decoys are on topic: even a perfect relevance filter loses 23 to 31 points to rarest-first selection in the classic hidden-profile configuration. Rarest-first selection is no better than random selection on average and wins only where the rare facts happen to be the useful ones. In both cases accuracy follows the balance of evidence the memory keeps, not the policy that kept it. The decision model adds a third failure, a form of social proof: it gives extra weight to facts attributed to many agents. Removing the attribution tags, or reassigning them at random with line order fixed, raises accuracy in the classic configuration by 13 to 24 points. In natural discussions the evidence is lost before any memory acts: the complete transcript yields lower accuracy than no notes at all.

item.title: Beyond Greenwashing: Algorithmic Resilience and the Non-Linear Governance Premium in Sovereign Capital Flows [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.35895v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Despite the proliferation of sovereign Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) metrics, traditional linear macro-financial models systematically misprice Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) tail risks during systemic shocks. This paper demonstrates that sovereign risk transmission is fundamentally non-linear. Using a forward-chained global panel of 147 sovereign entities (2010-2024), we deploy a gradient boosting architecture that compresses forecast errors by over 39% against L1-regularized baselines precisely during extreme macroeconomic tail events. Moving beyond opaque predictive accuracy, we apply dual interpretability frameworks to mathematically map the discrete threshold effects of institutional quality. We identify a strict, non-linear "Governance Premium": incremental environmental and social improvements yield zero capital advantage until a foundational regulatory threshold is breached. Finally, we establish regime-conditional 95% uncertainty bounds that maintain valid marginal coverage even under severe ESG reporting failures. This framework equips policymakers with a distribution-free tool to quantify sovereign tail-risk, proving that global capital markets price institutional resilience as a discrete boundary rather than a continuous premium.

item.title: Physiognomy Revisited: How Vision-Language Models Encode Sensitive Attributes Through Image Transformation [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.35910v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Emergent generative AI technologies, while remarkably beneficial across several tasks and domains, can suffer from unforeseen vulnerabilities and difficult-to-anticipate failure modes. Such failure modes can disparately affect vulnerable communities. This paper investigates two well-known vision language models (VLMs) and inspects how these models encode protected identities while generating images. We show that when VLMs are requested to transform human face images to reflect race identities (e.g., Hispanic, Black, White, or Asian) and sexual orientation (e.g., gay or straight), VLMs often comply with such requests. We demonstrate that compliance (and refusal) is non-deterministic, group-sensitive, and generated images are statistically distinguishable, often accentuating deep-seated stereotypes. We further show that representation biases introduced during image generation can re-emerge in textual reasoning and characterization tasks. Finally, we show that this worrisome finding is not limited to racial identity or sexual orientation, image generation can perpetuate bias around criminality, raising concerning possibilities of AI-assisted profiling.

item.title: ReCoPII: A Relation-Grounded Framework for Building Contextual PII Masking Datasets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.35925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training contextual masking systems for personally identifiable information (PII) requires examples distinguishing maskable from preservable mentions of one entity type, but privacy restrictions limit access to real data. Author-based augmentation (SPY) labels mentions unrelated to the author as non-PII, presuming a single data subject and overlooking others. We propose ReCoPII (Relation-grounded Contextual PII masking), a framework that builds such data without this premise: it plans ontology-constrained entity relations, writes insertion sentences with placeholders, reconstructs annotations with code, checks the result with a separate LLM, and derives MASK/KEEP labels from entity relations. On Korean documents from six domains, it yields ReCoPII-Ko, a corpus with relation, privacy, and MASK/KEEP annotations, which we validate. Across 300 pairs, four annotators agree with 88.42% of its sampled KEEP labels, against 26.27% for SPY-style augmentation of the same sources. Classifiers trained on it over-mask less than under that reference on a matched test. Contextual masking fine-tuned jointly with a PII detector removes most over-masking of detection alone within a fixed leakage budget; on human-verified entity records, the four detectors meeting it over-mask at most 5.04% with at most 4.18% leakage. The detector is comparable to XLM-R-large on KDPII with about a quarter of its parameters.

item.title: SCOPE: Source Credibility and Outlet Profiling Engine [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.35929v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present SCOPE, a multi-agent system for profiling news media outlets with respect to bias, factuality, and credibility. Given an outlet URL, SCOPE coordinates specialized agents for article acquisition, content analysis, external evidence search, scoring, and report generation. The system follows an MBFC-style methodology while making intermediate evidence and agent outputs inspectable through a structured demonstration interface. On a benchmark of 200 media outlets, SCOPE outperforms LLM-only, article-only, search-only, and media-background-check baselines on most metrics, achieving the lowest bias and factuality MAE, perfect failed-fact-check detection, and the lowest factual error rate. These results suggest that decomposed, evidence-grounded agent workflows can support more transparent and reliable media profiling. Our code is available at https://github.com/mbaisbay/SCOPE, and a live demonstration at https://scope-demo.streamlit.app/.

item.title: Curriculum-Driven Deep Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Far-Range Rocket Landing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.35954v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous vertical landing of reusable launch vehicles is a critical yet formidable challenge in aerospace engineering, primarily due to highly nonlinear dynamics, stringent precision require- ments, and inherent environmental uncertainties. While reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising alternative to traditional model-based control, existing approaches frequently rely on flat training paradigms and highly simplified initial conditions, drastically limiting their real-world applicability. This paper proposes a comprehensive curriculum-driven deep reinforcement learning framework designed to master both far-range navigation and precision landing. By employing a three-stage curriculum augmented with a critic warm-up procedure and a rehearsal mechanism to prevent catastrophic forgetting, alongside a high-dimensional observation vector utilizing a full 3 X 3 rotation-matrix, the agent is trained to navigate from an initial horizontal distance of 1,000 to 1,500 units vastly farther than prior benchmarks before executing a soft touchdown. Crucially, we intro- duce a redesigned reward function that reduces unnecessary computational overhead and addresses limitations of earlier formulations, including poorly calibrated reward components and potentially conflicting optimization objectives. The redesigned function bounds the per-step reward magnitude by (O(1)), while its progress term accumulates the total distance closed over the trajectory. The available 100,000-episode results report a 99.98% success rate for the proposed policy and 68.31% for the baseline under the evaluation conditions. In the evaluation, the proposed policy retained 69.1% of its initial fuel capacity and achieved a mean final distance from the pad centre of 7.07 units, compared with 13.10 units for the baseline. Landing visualizations are available in Video 1 and Video 2.

item.title: ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.35955v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-bit weight--activation quantization reduces the memory and computation needed to deploy large language models, but activation rounding can still degrade accuracy after calibration. Reconstruction from rounded inputs cannot distinguish activations within the same quantization bin. We propose ResCom, a low-rank correction that uses the activation rounding residual to compensate for the resulting layer-output error. An output-aware calibration procedure selects residual directions by their contribution to output reconstruction and computes the correction in closed form, without gradient training or updates to the calibrated weights. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weights and activations, rank-32 attention corrections reduce WikiText-2 perplexity from 7.708 to 7.147, improve MMLU by 2.89 percentage points, and raise five-shot GSM8K accuracy from 23.96 to 36.16 percent. Evaluations on models from 1B to 70B parameters and on held-out C4 test the method beyond this setting. The evaluated FP32 implementation adds 2.25 percent to 4K prefill time; a separate compact-storage implementation retains a 27.7 percent peak-memory reduction relative to FP16.

item.title: Multiple Leak Localization in Water Distribution Networks through Graph Neural Networks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.35972v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Leak localization in water distribution networks is challenging when multiple leaks occur simultaneously, particularly under sparse monitoring. Existing data-driven methods often assume a single or predefined number of leaks or require extensive enumeration of leak combinations. This study proposes a graph neural network (GNN) model that localizes a variable number of simultaneous leaks without specifying the leak count in advance or exhaustively generating every possible combination of leak locations for training. The model is evaluated on two benchmark networks of different sizes, the 31-node Hanoi network and the larger 92-node NET3 network, under variable demand, sparse pressure-sensor coverage, variable leak magnitudes, and varying numbers of simultaneous leaks. The GNN outperforms multilayer perceptron, support vector machine, K-nearest neighbors, and random forest classifiers by up to 12% and 20% in accuracy respectively in Hanoi and NET3 networks. Consistent performance across both networks supports the scalability of the proposed approach.

item.title: UnityBench-Mini3D: Evaluating LLM Agents for 3D Game Development in Unity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.35980v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Game development stresses coding agents in ways general software engineering does not: correctness depends on how engine APIs, serialized scene state, and runtime behavior interact, not on source code alone. Existing benchmarks mainly target platforms such as Godot and heavily rely on LLM judges or coarse task-level outcomes. We present UnityBench-Mini3D, a benchmark of 77 project-level Unity tasks organized around seven expert-defined skill categories rather than tutorials or genres, with three difficulty tiers. Each task pairs a complete Unity project with natural-language requirements and is evaluated using 1,178 held-out, human-authored milestone tests covering scene structure, component configuration, and runtime behavior. This in-engine evaluation provides deterministic partial credit, localizes failures, and distinguishes partial implementations from complete solutions without relying on subjective judges. Across 21 models and 9 coding harnesses, the average pass rate reaches 80.9% on easy tasks but falls to 35.2% on hard tasks, with just 57.7% overall. UnityBench-Mini3D provides a reproducible, diagnostic testbed distinguishing systems across difficulty levels.

item.title: Let the Gate Decide: Per-Lookup Precision for Quantized Conditional Memory in LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.35985v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conditional memory layers, such as DeepSeek's Engram, attach large hashed n-gram tables to a language model, and removing them from DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash costs 36.8 PopQA points. Low-bit quantization loses long-tail facts first, and the standard remedy, giving more bits to frequently accessed rows, backfires: refining lookups by access frequency is worse than refining them at random. We trace this to the gate that scales each retrieved row. A lookup's quantization error is weighted by its gate, which is small for frequent n-grams, large for the rare n-grams of long-tail entities, and computable from a 1-bit code. GateRQ therefore stores each row as a ladder of 1-bit residual codes, keeps level 1 in GPU memory to compute the gate, and reads deeper levels only for the lookups the gate ranks highest. Without retraining, GateRQ cuts GPU table memory by 7.8x on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, which raises vLLM throughput by 11%-31% over FP8 tables, while losing about 1 PopQA point at 1.50 bits read per lookup and 0.2 points at 2.10 bits across two models.

item.title: PROBE: Frontier Coding Agents Find Different Bugs Than Maintainers Fix [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.35987v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Proactive bug discovery is an important software-engineering problem. Even though coding agents are already widely deployed in this domain, their capabilities remain understudied. In particular, the challenging task of finding all bugs that human maintainers would repair across an entire repository has not been studied yet. To close this gap, we introduce PROBE, a benchmark consisting of all 2,457 bugs fixed over the course of 18 months across 20 diverse GitHub repositories, together with a method for matching candidate findings to this partial reference set. We evaluate coding agents across frontier models and find they all achieve a recall of below $21\%$ and a precision of less than $9\%$ with respect to the reference set. While stronger models increase recall substantially from $8\%$ to $17\%$, they do not improve precision. Surprisingly, despite the low precision, LLM and human evaluators still judge $85\%$ of findings valid. Crucially, we find that found bug distributions are similar across agents but differ substantially from those of bugs fixed by maintainers. The practical relevance of bug discovery and the low recall of frontier models make this benchmark a valuable resource for both model users and developers.

item.title: Layerwise Repacking: Variable-Length Hybrid-Attention Training without an Extra Redistribution Pass [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.35989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Variable-length training creates conflicting parallelism requirements across the layers of a hybrid-attention model. The longest samples require wide sequence-parallel (SP) groups of 16 or 32 ranks for full attention, whose cost grows quadratically with sequence length. Sparse-attention layers, dominated by near-linear MoE work, can instead balance most evaluated workloads within node-local SP8 groups. Reusing the wide groups for these layers pushes their all-to-all communication across nodes, where the observed effective rate is 7.0x lower. Yet switching to smaller groups changes which ranks own each sample; a separate redistribution at every full-sparse boundary would introduce another data transfer. Layerwise Repacking keeps each SP16/32 parent for full attention and repacks its samples into node-local sparse children at SP{1, 2, 4, 8}, where hidden states persist between full layers. The layout change rides on the two existing full-layer Ulysses sites: at each, one variable-size all-to-all performs both the head exchange and the sample repacking, so no redistribution pass is added. Because the balance the children can reach depends on which samples share a parent, an auxiliary parent solver rebalances parent membership before the children are formed. On all 22 steps with SP16/32 parents among the first 200 training steps of a 1F3S hybrid-attention model (one full-attention layer per three sparse-attention layers), repacking alone reduces the mean end-to-end time by 5.95% and raises model FLOPs utilization (MFU) by 3.75 percentage points over the baseline with repacking disabled; with the improved solver, end-to-end time falls by 7.61% and MFU rises by 4.83 percentage points.

item.title: DuplexTune: Coupled-State Replay for Memory-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Adaptation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36009v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse expert execution does not remove the stored states needed to adapt a mixture-of-experts language model. We present DuplexTune, a framework for replaying coupled hidden states through pretrained attention and expert modules. Trainable width bridges connect two residual streams to the backbone. Bridge warm-up precedes backbone adaptation, with router weights kept frozen. We analyze the implicit state-recovery equation and identify the convergence and replay conditions needed for reconstruction. On Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, the single-H800 evaluation reports 38.8 GB peak memory, versus 64.8 GB for supervised fine-tuning with checkpointing, and throughput of 25.1 versus 19.9 samples/s. DuplexTune achieves 67.2% MMLU, 75.6% GSM8K, and 7.69 MT-Bench, with a weaker multilingual score than the checkpointed baseline. The results characterize a configuration-dependent tradeoff among state storage, throughput, and adaptation quality.

item.title: Rollback: Experience Backtracking in World Models for Policy Improvement [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36068v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Action-conditioned world models offer a scalable alternative to costly real-world interaction for improving robot policies. However, existing world-model-based methods largely treat world models as forward-only surrogates of the physical environment, leaving untapped a capability no physical environment affords: rewinding to past decision points to explore counterfactual futures. We introduce Rollback, a policy improvement paradigm that turns world models from passive simulators into counterfactual engines: it rolls back to critical decision points, branches into alternative actions, and contrasts their outcomes to attribute success to individual decisions. This concentrates imagination where it matters most and distills counterfactual outcomes into fine-grained, action-level supervision without a separately learned value model. We build a scalable training system that unifies distributed world-model search with asynchronous real-robot execution, forming a self-reinforcing cycle: real-world experience continually sharpens the world model, and a sharper world model in turn drives further policy improvement. We term the world-model side of this cycle test-time physics grounding, a capability that hand-built physics simulators lack: while the world model serves as the training environment, real transitions from the policy it trains correct its dynamics through a lightweight LoRA pipeline. Experiments on three challenging real-world tasks show that Rollback improves success rates over the strongest baseline by an absolute 10.67%, 11.11%, and 11.85% on block extraction, ball tossing, and tabletop curling, respectively, while achieving more stable improvement throughout training. Although initialized from teleoperated demonstrations far below human level, Rollback surpasses the average success rate of human players on both ball tossing and tabletop curling within 8 hours of training.

item.title: Dirichlet Process Mixtures within Semiparametric Bayesian Networks: A Novel Conditional Density Estimation Approach [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36110v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Semiparametric Bayesian networks (SPBNs) are flexible probabilistic graphical models for representing joint distributions of continuous variables through lower-dimensional conditional probability distributions (CPDs). Existing SPBN models use kernel density estimators (KDEs) for non-parametric CPD modeling, but their one-component-per-observation mixture representation can lead to increased inference costs and density estimation errors, which can be limiting. In this work, we define a new CPD modeling approach for non-parametric components based on Bayesian non-parametric Dirichlet Process Mixtures (DPMs) within SPBNs. DPMs provide a data-adaptive clustering of observations, yielding a more compact representation while retaining the flexibility of non-parametric density estimation, unlike KDE. This results in lower inference costs while improving density estimation performance. We implement the proposed DPM-based SPBN (DPM-SPBN) by extending the open-source PyBNesian package and evaluate it on synthetic and real-world data. For a given network structure, DPM-based CPDs significantly outperform state-of-the-art Bayesian network models for continuous variables in density estimation, achieving lower absolute log-likelihood errors on synthetic data. We further investigate the impact of the proposed CPD modeling on structure learning methods relying on CPD-based scores. DPM-based SPBNs achieve lower structure learning and density estimation errors than KDE-based SPBNs. Experiments on real-world data corroborate these findings, identifying DPM-based CPD modeling as the most effective alternative among the evaluated non-parametric approaches for continuous variables.

item.title: Scaling and Renormalization in Neural Networks: An Effective Renormalization-Group Description of Grokking [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Grokking is a delayed transition from memorization to generalization in deep neural networks (NNs). We examine whether scaling and renormalization group (RG) theories can describe this dynamics, establishing a quantitative physical framework for neural generalization transitions.
